etymology: From the Latin divortium, “a turning apart,” through the Old French divorce, with the English suffix -ment denoting the act or the instrument of it; in the Authorized Version it renders the Hebrew kērīthūth (a cutting off) and the Greek apostasion, the written deed of severance.
biblical_def: Divorcement is the formal putting away of a wife by a written deed. The word enters Scripture not as a gift but as a restraint: “then let him write her a bill of divorcement, and give it in her hand, and send her out of his house” (Deu 24:1). Moses did not institute the practice; he found it and bridled it, requiring a public document, a delivery into her hand, and a bar upon the first husband ever taking her again (Deu 24:4). The paper protected the woman and slowed the man. Our Lord Himself settles the question of what that statute meant. When the Pharisees pressed Him — “Why did Moses then command to give a writing of divorcement?” (Mat 19:7) — He answered that Moses suffered it “because of the hardness of your hearts: but from the beginning it was not so” (Mat 19:8), and He sent them back past Sinai to Eden: one man, one woman, one flesh, and “what therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder” (Mat 19:6; Gen 2:24). A concession to hardness is not a licence to be hard. Isaiah turns the word to the LORD’s own use and demands the document be produced: “Where is the bill of your mother’s divorcement, whom I have put away?” (Isa 50:1). There is none, for He has not put His covenant people away; they sold themselves. The covenant God keeps is the pattern for the covenant of marriage.
webster_summary: The legal dissolution of the marriage bond, and the written instrument by which it was declared; in Scripture a Mosaic restraint upon hardness of heart, not a permission.
webster_full: DIVORCEMENT, dissolution of the bond of marriage; the act of putting away a wife, or the writing which declares it.
From the Latin divortium, a turning apart, from divertere, to turn aside.
In the Mosaic law the bill of divorcement was required in writing and delivered into the woman’s hand (Deu 24:1).
The word is used figuratively of the LORD’s dealings with Israel, whom He chastens but does not finally put away (Isa 50:1).
It is distinguished from separation, which suspends cohabitation without pretending to dissolve the bond.
scriptures: Deu 24:1

When a man hath taken a wife, and married her, and it come to pass that she find no favour in his eyes, because he hath found some uncleanness in her: then let him write her a bill of divorcement, and give it in her hand, and send her out of his house.
Mat 19:8
He saith unto them, Moses because of the hardness of your hearts suffered you to put away your wives: but from the beginning it was not so.
Mat 19:6
Wherefore they are no more twain, but one flesh. What therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder.
Isa 50:1

Thus saith the LORD, Where is the bill of your mother's divorcement, whom I have put away? or which of my creditors is it to whom I have sold you? Behold, for your iniquities have ye sold yourselves, and for your transgressions is your mother put away.
corruption_summary: No-fault divorce has taken a Mosaic restraint upon hardness of heart and made it the ordinary machinery of a culture that treats the marriage covenant as dissoluble at will.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern corruption is not that men divorce — men have always been hard — but that the law and the church together have stopped calling it what it is. The no-fault statutes that swept the American states from 1969 onward removed the requirement of any wrong at all: one party’s unwillingness now dissolves what two swore before God to keep. The governing phrase, irreconcilable differences, is a masterpiece of evasion; it names no sin, accuses no one, and quietly asserts that a covenant is a preference. Scripture will not have it. “For the LORD, the God of Israel, saith that he hateth putting away” (Mal 2:16), and the Lord Jesus grounds marriage not in the satisfaction of the parties but in the act of God: “What therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder” (Mat 19:6). Where Christ allows a narrow exception it is for fornication (Mat 19:9), and the apostle adds the desertion of an unbelieving spouse (1Co 7:15) — grounds, not moods. A marriage is not ended because it has ceased to please.

Notice also what the deed itself was for. The bill of divorcement was a burden laid on the man: he must write, and witness, and deliver, and he could never undo it and take her back (Deu 24:4). Moses put friction into the thing precisely because hard hearts move fast. Modern practice inverts the statute — the paperwork is now the easiest part of the transaction, filed online, uncontested, no cause alleged. And when the church absorbs that instinct and preaches divorce as an act of self-care, it is preaching the hardness Moses restrained. Recover the older order: marriage is one man and one woman covenanting before God for life (Gen 2:24); repentance and forgiveness are the ordinary remedy for the offences of a marriage; and the God who was provoked by Israel a thousand years and still would not produce the bill (Isa 50:1) is the pattern for husbands who have been sinned against.
roots_summary: Hebrew kērīthūth, a cutting off; Greek apostasion, a standing away — both name a severance, and both are used of a written deed.
roots_lines: Hebrew kērīthūth (H3748) — a cutting, a severance; from kārath, to cut — the same verb used for cutting a covenant.
Greek apostasion (G647) — a standing off, hence the certificate of repudiation (Mat 5:31; Mat 19:7; Mar 10:4).
The Authorized Version renders the Hebrew phrase “bill of divorcement” and the Greek variously “writing of divorcement” and “bill of divorcement.”
That kārath both cuts a covenant and cuts one off is not accident: the same knife that binds can sever, and Scripture keeps the sobering echo.
Latin divortium underlies the English word — a turning apart of two who had gone one way.
usage: Of the Mosaic statute restraining a hard husband: the bill required, the woman protected, the return forbidden (Deu 24:1–4).
Of our Lord’s exposition, which sends the question back past Moses to the creation ordinance (Mat 19:4–9; Mar 10:2–12).
Figuratively of the LORD and His covenant people, where the demanded bill cannot be produced because He has not finally put her away (Isa 50:1).

etymology: From the Middle English bille, through the Anglo-Latin billa, a variant of bulla, “a seal or sealed document”; hence any written instrument — a deed, a bond, an account of debt — whose force lies in its being written and delivered.
biblical_def: A bill in the Authorized Version is a written legal instrument: a document that fixes in ink what would otherwise be a man’s changeable word. It appears in two settings. The first is the marriage law, where the hard husband is required to “write her a bill of divorcement, and give it in her hand” (Deu 24:1) — and the requirement is the mercy in it, for the writing takes time, the delivery is public, and the deed can never be recalled (Deu 24:4). The second is the counting-house, where the unjust steward calls in his lord’s debtors and says, “Take thy bill, and sit down quickly, and write fifty” (Luk 16:6). There the bill is the record of what a man owes, and the whole force of the parable turns on the fact that a written obligation is a real one. Scripture then lifts the word. Isaiah has the LORD challenge His people to produce the deed of their mother’s severance: “Where is the bill of your mother’s divorcement, whom I have put away?” (Isa 50:1). No such paper exists. And in Jeremiah the LORD, having borne with backsliding Israel, says He “had put her away, and given her a bill of divorce” (Jer 3:8) — the covenant God who does nothing arbitrarily, whose severances are documented and just. Behind every biblical bill stands the truth that God keeps records.
webster_summary: A written instrument — a deed, bond, or account of debt; in Scripture the bill of divorcement and the debtor’s bill, both binding because written.
webster_full: BILL, a written paper containing a statement of particulars; an account of goods sold, or of debt due.
In law, a declaration in writing, expressing some wrong the complainant hath suffered, or a fault committed by some person.
A bill of divorce, a writing given by a husband to his wife, declaring the marriage dissolved (Deu 24:1).
From the Anglo-Latin billa, a variant of bulla, a seal — whence also the papal bull, a sealed instrument.
Distinguished from a bond by requiring no surety, and from a note by being a statement of particulars.
scriptures: Deu 24:1

When a man hath taken a wife, and married her, and it come to pass that she find no favour in his eyes, because he hath found some uncleanness in her: then let him write her a bill of divorcement, and give it in her hand, and send her out of his house.
Mar 10:4
And they said, Moses suffered to write a bill of divorcement, and to put her away.
Luk 16:6
And he said, An hundred measures of oil. And he said unto him, Take thy bill, and sit down quickly, and write fifty.
Jer 3:8

And I saw, when for all the causes whereby backsliding Israel committed adultery I had put her away, and given her a bill of divorce; yet her treacherous sister Judah feared not, but went and played the harlot also.
corruption_summary: The modern instinct treats the paperwork as the permission — if a thing can be lawfully filed, it must be lawfully done; Scripture makes the written deed a restraint upon sin, never a warrant for it.
corruption_paragraphs: The live corruption around this small word is the confusion of legality with lawfulness. Moses required a bill so that a man could not put away his wife in a fit of temper on a Tuesday and take her back on a Thursday; the document was friction, witness, and finality. The modern mind reads the same statute backwards and concludes that because the law provided a form, the law approved the act. Our Lord forecloses that reading exactly: Moses suffered it “because of the hardness of your hearts” (Mat 19:8; Mar 10:5). A permission granted to restrain an evil is not a blessing pronounced upon it. The same error runs through a hundred modern questions — the state issues a licence, files a certificate, stamps a form, and the conscience quiets itself on the strength of the stamp. But no civil registry can make lawful what God has forbidden, and no filed instrument can dissolve what God has joined (Mat 19:6).

The second corruption is subtler and belongs to the counting-house. The steward’s bills in Luke 16 are records of real debt, and his crime is that he alters them — fifty for a hundred, fourscore for a hundred — with another man’s goods. A culture that regards every written obligation as renegotiable, every contract as a starting position, every debt as a grievance, has learned the steward’s trade and forgotten his Lord’s ledger. Scripture’s comfort is not that the bill is fictitious but that it has been paid: the handwriting of ordinances that was against us Christ took out of the way, nailing it to His cross (Col 2:14). That is the only cancellation of a bill the gospel offers, and it cost blood. Recover the plain principle: a written word binds, God keeps accounts, and the debt is discharged by satisfaction, not by amendment.
roots_summary: English bill from Anglo-Latin billa, a sealed document; it renders Hebrew sēpher, a writing, and Greek gramma, a written thing.
roots_lines: Hebrew sēpher (H5612) — a writing, book, scroll, or legal document; in Deu 24:1 the sēpher kērīthūth, the writing of severance.
Greek gramma (G1121) — a letter, a written record; the steward’s grammata are the account-books of Luk 16:6–7.
Greek apostasion (G647) is also rendered “bill of divorcement” in Mar 10:4.
Anglo-Latin billa from bulla, a seal or boss — the seal, not the ink, was what once made a paper binding.
The Reformers seized the ledger figure gladly: Christ blots out the handwriting that stood against us (Col 2:14).
usage: Of the written deed of severance in the marriage law and in our Lord’s exposition of it (Deu 24:1; Mar 10:4).
Of a record of debt in the parable of the unjust steward, altered by a servant with his lord’s goods (Luk 16:6–7).
Figuratively of the LORD’s covenant dealings — the bill He gave backsliding Israel (Jer 3:8), and the bill Judah cannot produce (Isa 50:1).

etymology: From the Old French revengier, “to avenge,” from the Latin vindicare, to claim or lay claim to, hence to vindicate; the revenger is the one who lays claim on behalf of another — in Scripture, the kinsman who claims the blood of the slain.
biblical_def: The revenger of blood, the gō’ēl haddām, is the nearest kinsman of a murdered man, charged under the Mosaic law with executing the sentence upon the murderer: “The revenger of blood himself shall slay the murderer: when he meeteth him, he shall slay him” (Num 35:19). This is not private vendetta but public justice lodged in the family’s hand before Israel had settled courts in every gate. The sixth commandment stands behind it: manslaying is not a private grief to be settled by payment, for man is made in the image of God, and the blood of the slain cries from the ground (Gen 9:6; Gen 4:10). Yet the same law that arms the revenger also bridles him. Six cities of refuge are appointed, and the slayer who killed unawares may flee to one of them; there “the congregation shall judge between the slayer and the revenger of blood” (Num 35:24), and if he is found guiltless of murder they deliver him out of the revenger’s hand and restore him to the city (Num 35:25). Justice is not left to a hot heart. The New Testament carries the office forward into the civil magistrate: he “beareth not the sword in vain: for he is the minister of God, a revenger to execute wrath upon him that doeth evil” (Rom 13:4). Vengeance belongs to God, and He administers it through appointed hands.
webster_summary: One who avenges; in the Mosaic law the nearest kinsman charged to execute the murderer, and in the New Testament the civil magistrate bearing the sword as God’s minister.
webster_full: REVENGER, one who revenges; one who avenges another, or executes just vengeance upon a wrong.
From the Old French revengier, and ultimately the Latin vindicare, to vindicate or lay claim.
In the Hebrew polity, the avenger of blood was the next of kin to the slain, whose duty it was to pursue the manslayer (Num 35:19).
The cities of refuge were appointed to shelter him that killed unawares until the congregation had judged the case (Num 35:24–25).
Applied by the apostle to the civil ruler, who beareth the sword as the minister of God (Rom 13:4).
scriptures: The revenger of blood himself shall slay the murderer: when he meeteth him, he shall slay him.
Then the congregation shall judge between the slayer and the revenger of blood according to these judgments:

And the congregation shall deliver the slayer out of the hand of the revenger of blood, and the congregation shall restore him to the city of his refuge, whither he was fled: and he shall abide in it unto the death of the high priest, which was anointed with the holy oil.
Rom 13:4

For he is the minister of God to thee for good. But if thou do that which is evil, be afraid; for he beareth not the sword in vain: for he is the minister of God, a revenger to execute wrath upon him that doeth evil.
corruption_summary: Two errors meet at this word: the private vengeance that seizes the sword God gave the magistrate, and the sentimental abolition of retribution altogether, which leaves the blood of the slain uncried-for.
corruption_paragraphs: The first corruption is the vigilante instinct — the man who reads Num 35:19 as a warrant for settling his own accounts. It cannot be read so. The very chapter that arms the revenger builds six cities to outrun him, requires a congregation to judge between him and the slayer, and forbids his hand while the accused stands within the walls (Num 35:12, 24–25). The office is an office, hedged with process, not a licence for wrath. And the apostle plainly transfers the sword from the kinsman to the magistrate: “Dearly beloved, avenge not yourselves, but rather give place unto wrath: for it is written, Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord” (Rom 12:19), and immediately after names the ruler God’s revenger (Rom 13:4). The Christian is forbidden the sword he is commanded to honor in another’s hand.

The opposite corruption is now the louder one: that retribution as such is barbarous, that punishment must be justified only as deterrence or as the reform of the offender, and that a state which executes a murderer has itself committed murder. This empties Rom 13:4 of its plain sense and, worse, empties the sixth commandment of its sanction. Scripture grounds the death penalty for murder not in social utility but in the image of God: “Whoso sheddeth man’s blood, by man shall his blood be shed: for in the image of God made he man” (Gen 9:6). Precisely because the victim was an image-bearer, his blood may not be shrugged off. Where the magistrate refuses the sword he was given, he does not become merciful; he becomes negligent, and the innocent pay for it. Recover the whole doctrine: vengeance is God’s, He administers it through the magistrate, the process must be just and witnessed, and mercy toward the guilty is God’s prerogative in the gospel, not the state’s duty at the bar.
roots_summary: Hebrew gō’ēl, the kinsman-redeemer, is the same word for the revenger of blood — the nearest kin both ransoms and requites.
roots_lines: Hebrew gō’ēl (H1350) — the near kinsman who redeems; joined to dām, blood, it is the revenger of blood (Num 35:19).
The same root makes Boaz the gō’ēl of Ruth and gives Job his cry, “I know that my redeemer liveth” (Job 19:25).
Hebrew nāqam (H5358) — to avenge, requite; the noun nāqām is the vengeance the LORD reserves to Himself (Deu 32:35).
Greek ekdikos (G1558) — one who carries justice out from the law; the magistrate of Rom 13:4.
That one Hebrew word carries both redemption and requital is a mercy to meditate on: the Kinsman who claims our blood is the Kinsman who paid it.
usage: Of the nearest kinsman under the Mosaic law, charged to execute the murderer but barred from the man within the city of refuge (Num 35:19, 25).
Of the congregation’s duty to judge between revenger and slayer, distinguishing murder from manslaughter (Num 35:24).
Of the civil magistrate as God’s appointed minister bearing the sword against evildoers (Rom 13:4).

biblical_def: In the Authorized Version slayer is a term of art. It does not mean simply one who has killed; it names the man who has taken a life without malice — “which killeth any person at unawares” (Num 35:11) — and who therefore has a refuge to flee to. The murderer has none: “the revenger of blood himself shall slay the murderer” (Num 35:19). Between these two the law of God draws a bright line that the sixth commandment requires and that every just legal order since has borrowed. Six cities were set apart, three on each side of Jordan, and the roads to them prepared, “that every slayer may flee thither” (Deu 19:3). There he was safe from the hot heart of the avenger until the congregation could judge the case (Num 35:24), and if judged guiltless of murder he abode in the city “unto the death of the high priest” (Num 35:25), whose death released him to his inheritance. The type is unmistakable. The sinner, pursued by a justice he cannot outrun, flees to a refuge appointed by God, and is held there by a High Priest whose death is his liberty. So the writer to the Hebrews speaks of those “who have fled for refuge to lay hold upon the hope set before us” (Heb 6:18). The slayer’s road is the sinner’s road, and Christ is at the end of it.
etymology: From the Old English slean, “to strike, to smite,” whence slay and the agent-noun slayer; in the Authorized Version it renders the Hebrew participle rōtzēach used in its narrower sense of the man who has killed without lying in wait.
webster_summary: One who slays; in the Mosaic law specifically the manslayer who killed unawares and might flee to a city of refuge, as distinguished from the murderer.
webster_full: SLAYER, one who slays; a killer; a murderer; one who kills a person with or without malice.
From the Old English slean, to smite or strike, of the same stock as the German schlagen.
In the Hebrew law the slayer is distinguished from the murderer by the absence of hatred and of lying in wait (Deu 19:3–6; Jos 20:3).
The cities of refuge were appointed for the slayer, that he might live until the congregation had judged his cause.
He abode in the city of refuge until the death of the high priest, and then returned to his own possession.
scriptures: Then ye shall appoint you cities to be cities of refuge for you; that the slayer may flee thither, which killeth any person at unawares.
Deu 19:3
Thou shalt prepare thee a way, and divide the coasts of thy land, which the LORD thy God giveth thee to inherit, into three parts, that every slayer may flee thither.
Jos 20:3
That the slayer that killeth any person unawares and unwittingly may flee thither: and they shall be your refuge from the avenger of blood.
Heb 6:18
That by two immutable things, in which it was impossible for God to lie, we might have a strong consolation, who have fled for refuge to lay hold upon the hope set before us:
corruption_summary: Modern practice erodes the very distinction the slayer statutes exist to make — sometimes flattening intent away, sometimes excusing malice as circumstance — and so loses the sixth commandment’s precision.
corruption_paragraphs: The law of the slayer is God’s own instruction in the difference between murder and manslaughter, and both errors that assail it are errors about the heart. On one side lies the flattening of intent: a killing is a killing, the outcome is all, and the man who struck by accident is handled as the man who lay in wait. Scripture refuses this. The test it gives is inward and specific — the slayer “hated him not in time past,” he did not thrust of enmity, he did not hurl anything at him by laying of wait (Num 35:20–23). Motive is not a modern legal nicety; it is a divine category, because the Judge of all the earth reads the heart. On the other side lies the excusing of real malice as circumstance, upbringing, or provocation, until no one is a murderer and everyone is a product. That too Scripture refuses: “he is a murderer: the revenger of blood shall slay the murderer” (Num 35:21). The cities of refuge did not shelter the guilty; they made room for a hearing so that the guiltless would not die and the guilty would not escape.

There is a second and graver loss when the type is forgotten. The whole apparatus — the prepared roads, the open gates, the congregation’s judgment, the high priest’s death — was built to teach Israel the gospel in a figure. The man with blood on his hands runs for his life to a place God appointed, and it is not his innocence that keeps him but the walls; and it is not his merit that frees him but the death of the anointed priest (Num 35:25). Strip that away and the passage becomes an antiquarian note on ancient jurisprudence. Keep it, and every sinner who has ever fled to Christ knows the road. “We have fled for refuge to lay hold upon the hope set before us” (Heb 6:18) — and our High Priest has died, and we are free.
roots_summary: Hebrew rōtzēach covers both the murderer and the manslayer; the law, not the word, draws the line between them.
roots_lines: Hebrew rātzach (H7523) — to dash in pieces, to kill; the participle rōtzēach is rendered both “slayer” and “murderer.”
It is the verb of the sixth commandment: “Thou shalt not kill” (Exo 20:13) — that is, thou shalt not murder.
The distinguishing marks are given in Num 35:20–23: enmity, lying in wait, and hatred in time past.
Hebrew bishgāgāh, “in error, unawares” — the same word that governs the sin offering for unwitting sin (Lev 4).
Greek phoneus (G5406) carries the narrower New Testament sense of murderer (Rev 21:8).
usage: Of the manslayer who killed at unawares and had a right to the city of refuge (Num 35:11; Jos 20:3).
Of the case at law, where the congregation judges between the slayer and the revenger of blood (Num 35:24).
Typologically of the sinner fleeing to Christ, held safe until the death of the High Priest sets him free (Num 35:25; Heb 6:18).

etymology: From the Old English gylt, a crime or debt, with the privative suffix -less; hence “without guilt” — not merely feeling clear but standing clear, a verdict rather than a mood.
biblical_def: Guiltless is a forensic word. It describes not a man’s feelings about himself but his standing before a bar — and in Scripture the bar is God’s. Its most solemn appearance is the sanction of the third commandment: “Thou shalt not take the name of the LORD thy God in vain; for the LORD will not hold him guiltless that taketh his name in vain” (Exo 20:7). Men may hold the profane man guiltless; the Judge will not. That single clause tells us that guilt is not a social estimate but a divine reckoning, and that it persists whether or not anyone has noticed. The word runs the other way as well. David refuses to lift his hand against Saul and asks, “who can stretch forth his hand against the LORD’S anointed, and be guiltless?” (1Sa 26:9). Reuben and Gad are told they shall “be guiltless before the LORD, and before Israel” when their duty is discharged (Num 32:22). And our Lord, defending His disciples from the Pharisees’ sabbath charge, cuts to the heart of the matter: “if ye had known what this meaneth, I will have mercy, and not sacrifice, ye would not have condemned the guiltless” (Mat 12:7). The guiltless can be condemned by men. Only one verdict finally holds — and the gospel is that God justifies the ungodly, so that those who are not guiltless in themselves are declared righteous in Christ.
webster_summary: Free from guilt, crime, or offence; innocent as a matter of standing before the law and before God, not as a matter of feeling.
webster_full: GUILTLESS, free from guilt, crime, or offence; innocent.
From guilt, Old English gylt, a crime, a fault, a debt, with the negative termination -less.
It is used of exemption from the penalty of a law, as when the LORD declares He will not hold the profane guiltless (Exo 20:7).
It is also used of one acquitted of a charge unjustly brought, as our Saviour uses it of His disciples (Mat 12:7).
Distinguished from harmless, which respects the effect upon others, and from blameless, which respects reputation.
scriptures: Exo 20:7
Thou shalt not take the name of the LORD thy God in vain; for the LORD will not hold him guiltless that taketh his name in vain.
Mat 12:7
But if ye had known what this meaneth, I will have mercy, and not sacrifice, ye would not have condemned the guiltless.
And David said to Abishai, Destroy him not: for who can stretch forth his hand against the LORD'S anointed, and be guiltless?
And the land be subdued before the LORD: then afterward ye shall return, and be guiltless before the LORD, and before Israel; and this land shall be your possession before the LORD.
corruption_summary: Therapy culture has reduced guilt to a feeling to be managed and guiltlessness to a state of mind — erasing the courtroom, and with it the need for a Substitute.
corruption_paragraphs: The dominant modern treatment of guilt is not to deny it but to relocate it. Guilt becomes an emotion, a symptom, a residue of harsh upbringing or rigid religion, and the goal of care is to help a man stop feeling it. He is told his guilt is disproportionate, that he should not be so hard on himself, that shame is toxic and self-forgiveness is the cure. Every one of those sentences presupposes that guilt is inside the man. Scripture puts it outside him: guilt is a standing, a liability, a real relation to a real law and a real Judge. “Now we know that what things soever the law saith, it saith to them who are under the law: that every mouth may be stopped, and all the world may become guilty before God” (Rom 3:19). A stopped mouth is not a feeling. And David, who had every worldly reason to manage his conscience quietly, spoke instead to the only One whose verdict mattered: “Against thee, thee only, have I sinned, and done this evil in thy sight” (Psa 51:4). He asked not to feel better but to be washed.

The pastoral damage is exact and severe. If guilt is only a feeling, then the gospel is only reassurance, and Christ died to improve a mood. But if guilt is a verdict, then only a verdict can answer it — and that is precisely what justification is: God declaring the guilty righteous on the ground of a righteousness not their own, imputed to them, purchased by the obedience and blood of His Son. The third commandment’s sanction should be read exactly here. “The LORD will not hold him guiltless” (Exo 20:7) is terrible news until one sees that the LORD held His own Son guilty in the sinner’s room. Then the guiltless verdict comes, and it comes from the bench, not from the man. Recover the courtroom and the comfort returns with it: “Who shall lay any thing to the charge of God’s elect? It is God that justifieth” (Rom 8:33).
roots_summary: Hebrew nāqī, clean or acquitted; Greek anaitios, without cause of charge — both are courtroom words, not words of feeling.
roots_lines: Hebrew nāqāh (H5352) — to be clean, to be acquitted, to be held innocent; in Exo 20:7 the LORD “will not nāqāh” the profane.
Hebrew nāqī (H5355) — the adjective: clear, exempt from punishment, free of blood-guilt.
Greek anaitios (G338) — literally “without cause,” that is, having no charge that will stand; used twice in Mat 12 of the disciples.
The idea is uniformly juridical: to be guiltless is to have no case answerable against one, whatever one feels.
The same root gives Hebrew niqqāyōn, cleanness of hands (Psa 26:6) — innocence displayed, not merely claimed.
usage: Of the sanction attached to the third commandment, where God refuses to acquit the profaner of His name (Exo 20:7; Deu 5:11).
Of the innocent wrongly condemned by men, as our Lord’s disciples in the cornfield (Mat 12:7).
Of the discharge of a sworn duty, after which a man stands clear before God and before Israel (Num 32:22).

etymology: A native English compound, law + giver, coined to render the Hebrew mēchōqēq (the one who decrees, from the verb to inscribe or engrave) and the Greek nomothetēs, the setter-down of law.
biblical_def: A lawgiver is one who has authority to enact law, not merely to enforce it. Scripture uses the word sparingly and to great effect. Jacob’s dying prophecy sets it in the messianic line: “The sceptre shall not depart from Judah, nor a lawgiver from between his feet, until Shiloh come; and unto him shall the gathering of the people be” (Gen 49:10). Ruling authority is lodged in Judah’s house until the One comes to whom it belongs. Isaiah gathers the offices into a single confession of God: “For the LORD is our judge, the LORD is our lawgiver, the LORD is our king; he will save us” (Isa 33:22) — and the last clause is not an afterthought, for the very One who legislates is the One who rescues. Then James presses the point into the conscience: “There is one lawgiver, who is able to save and to destroy: who art thou that judgest another?” (Jas 4:12). The argument is precise. Because the power to bind the conscience belongs to the One who also holds the soul’s destiny, no creature may legislate for another creature’s conscience. Here is the ground of sola Scriptura and of Christian liberty at once: what God has not commanded, no man may require; what God has commanded, no man may excuse. Moses was a mediator of law, never its author.
webster_summary: One who enacts law; in Scripture supremely God Himself — the LORD our judge, lawgiver, and king, and the one lawgiver able to save and to destroy.
webster_full: LAWGIVER, one who makes or enacts a law; a legislator.
A compound of law and giver, answering to the Latin legislator.
In the Hebrew, mēchōqēq, one that decreeth, from a root signifying to engrave or inscribe — law being cut in stone.
It is applied to Judah as the seat of ruling authority (Gen 49:10; Psa 60:7), and to Moses as the mediator of the law given at Sinai.
It is applied absolutely to God, who alone has the right to bind the conscience (Isa 33:22; Jas 4:12).
scriptures: The sceptre shall not depart from Judah, nor a lawgiver from between his feet, until Shiloh come; and unto him shall the gathering of the people be.
Jas 4:12
There is one lawgiver, who is able to save and to destroy: who art thou that judgest another?
For the LORD is our judge, the LORD is our lawgiver, the LORD is our king; he will save us.
Psa 60:7
Gilead is mine, and Manasseh is mine; Ephraim also is the strength of mine head; Judah is my lawgiver;
corruption_summary: The modern age denies that there is any lawgiver over the conscience at all, enthroning personal autonomy as the highest good — while the church, from the other side, keeps binding consciences God has left free.
corruption_paragraphs: The reigning corruption is the doctrine of autonomy: that a man is a law to himself, that no authority outside the self may finally command him, and that the highest moral act is to live according to one’s own definition of the good. It is Eden’s offer in a modern accent — ye shall be as gods, knowing good and evil (Gen 3:5). James answers it in one sentence: “There is one lawgiver, who is able to save and to destroy” (Jas 4:12). The argument is not that God’s law is useful, or ancient, or widely held, but that the One who legislates is the One who holds your soul’s destiny in His hand, and there is no second. An autonomy that cannot save itself and cannot destroy itself has no business legislating for itself. Where this is denied, law becomes nothing but the preference of whoever has the votes, and no appeal above the majority remains — which is why the same century that abolished the divine Lawgiver produced the most lawless states in history.

The opposite error is the church’s own, and the Reformers named it plainly. Where a man — a pope, a council, a presbytery, a pastor, a conference platform — requires of the conscience what God has not required, he has usurped the office of the one lawgiver. This is the very hinge of sola Scriptura: Scripture alone binds the conscience absolutely, confessions bind subordinately as the church receives them, and every other counsel is advice. It is also the hinge of Christian liberty, which is not licence but freedom from man-made requirement in the things God has left indifferent (Rom 14; Col 2:20–23). Both errors are corrected by the same confession. Isaiah joins the offices and refuses to let them be parted: the LORD who is our lawgiver is our judge and our king, and — because it is He and no other — “he will save us” (Isa 33:22).
roots_summary: Hebrew mēchōqēq, from a root meaning to engrave; Greek nomothetēs, the one who sets down law.
roots_lines: Hebrew chāqaq (H2710) — to cut in, to inscribe, to decree; law is first of all something engraved.
Hebrew mēchōqēq (H2710, participle) — a decreer, a commander’s staff, a lawgiver (Gen 49:10; Num 21:18; Psa 60:7).
Greek nomothetēs (G3550) — from nomos, law, and tithēmi, to lay down; used once, of God alone (Jas 4:12).
The engraving root is why the Decalogue is written with the finger of God in tables of stone (Exo 31:18).
The same participle can denote the ruler’s staff itself, so that Gen 49:10 joins sceptre and lawgiver in one messianic promise.
usage: Of ruling authority lodged in Judah until Shiloh come — a messianic promise (Gen 49:10; Psa 60:7).
Of God absolutely, who is at once judge, lawgiver, king, and saviour of His people (Isa 33:22).
Of the one lawgiver whose sole authority over the conscience forbids us to judge one another by our own rules (Jas 4:12).

etymology: From the Latin seditio, literally “a going apart” (sed-, apart, and itio, a going) — the drawing away of a people from lawful authority; in the New Testament it renders the Greek stasis, a standing-off or faction, and dichostasia, a standing-in-two.
biblical_def: Sedition is the stirring up of a people against lawful authority — not the honest dissent of a subject, but the deliberate work of division and tumult. The Authorized Version uses it in three registers. First as a civil charge: Tertullus arraigns Paul before Felix as “a pestilent fellow, and a mover of sedition among all the Jews throughout the world” (Act 24:5) — a false charge, but a serious one, for sedition was a capital matter under Rome. Second, and most weightily, at the trial of our Lord. Barabbas is described as one “who for a certain sedition made in the city, and for murder, was cast into prison” (Luk 23:19), and Pilate “released unto them him that for sedition and murder was cast into prison, whom they had desired; but he delivered Jesus to their will” (Luk 23:25). The guilty seditionist walks free; the innocent Christ goes to the cross in his room. Substitution is enacted before the eyes of the world, in a courtyard, by a Roman governor who did not know what he was doing. Third, Paul lists “seditions” among the works of the flesh (Gal 5:20), setting the factious spirit alongside idolatry and witchcraft. The sin is not confined to the state; it is at home in the congregation, where the man who sows division is to be marked and avoided (Rom 16:17; Tit 3:10).
webster_summary: A factious commotion of the people; the stirring up of tumult or resistance against lawful authority, whether in the state or in the church.
webster_full: SEDITION, a factious commotion of the people, a tumultuous assembly of men rising in opposition to law or the administration of justice.
From the Latin seditio, a going apart or asunder, from sed, apart, and eo, itum, to go.
It is distinguished from treason, which is an attempt upon the sovereign power itself, and from mutiny, which is confined to soldiers or seamen.
In the New Testament it renders stasis, a standing off or insurrection, and is charged both truly against Barabbas and falsely against Paul.
It is reckoned among the works of the flesh, and so is a sin of the church as well as a crime of the state (Gal 5:20).
scriptures: (Who for a certain sedition made in the city, and for murder, was cast into prison.)
And he released unto them him that for sedition and murder was cast into prison, whom they had desired; but he delivered Jesus to their will.
Act 24:5
For we have found this man a pestilent fellow, and a mover of sedition among all the Jews throughout the world, and a ringleader of the sect of the Nazarenes:
Gal 5:20
Idolatry, witchcraft, hatred, variance, emulations, wrath, strife, seditions, heresies,
corruption_summary: The charge is corrupted from both ends: faithful preaching is arraigned as sedition, while the factious spirit inside the church is excused as courage.
corruption_paragraphs: The first corruption is as old as Tertullus. Name the sins of a ruling order and you will be charged with disturbing the peace — “a pestilent fellow, and a mover of sedition” (Act 24:5). Ahab greeted Elijah with the same accusation: “Art thou he that troubleth Israel?” (1Ki 18:17). The Christian answer is not to deny the authority but to distinguish the duty. Scripture commands honour and subjection to the magistrate as God’s minister (Rom 13:1–7; 1Pe 2:13–17), and Scripture equally commands, when the magistrate forbids what God requires, “We ought to obey God rather than men” (Act 5:29). That is not sedition; it is the refusal of a man’s claim to be the one lawgiver, and it is offered openly, without tumult, with the penalty accepted. The apostles preached and then went to prison singing. That is the pattern, and it is the opposite of the mob.

The second corruption is the churchly one, and it is more common among us. Paul reckons seditions — factions, standings-apart, party spirit — among the works of the flesh, in the same list as idolatry and witchcraft (Gal 5:20), and he tells the Romans to mark them which cause divisions and offences contrary to the doctrine they had learned (Rom 16:17). Yet the divisive man in a congregation is regularly excused as merely discerning, principled, a truth-teller among compromisers. Sometimes he is. Often he is a seditionist with a doctrinal vocabulary. The test is not the volume of his complaint but its substance and its channel: does he name a real departure from Scripture, and does he pursue it through the church’s appointed order, or does he gather a party in the parking lot? Recover the distinction, and both the martyr and the mischief-maker are correctly identified.
roots_summary: Latin seditio, a going apart; Greek stasis, a standing-off — both picture a body of people pulling away from its lawful head.
roots_lines: Latin seditio — from sed-, apart, and itio, a going: literally a walking away from lawful order.
Greek stasis (G4714) — a standing, hence a faction, insurrection, or riot (Luk 23:19; Act 24:5).
Greek dichostasia (G1370) — a standing in two; rendered “seditions” among the works of the flesh (Gal 5:20).
The imagery is bodily: a limb standing apart from the body is not independent, only severed.
Aramaic ’eshtaddūr, in Ezra’s correspondence, carries the same sense of a rebellious city — the charge levelled against rebuilt Jerusalem.
usage: Of the civil crime for which Barabbas was imprisoned and for which he was released in Christ’s room (Luk 23:19, 25).
Of the false charge brought against faithful preachers by those whose order their preaching disturbs (Act 24:5).
Of the factious, party-making spirit reckoned among the works of the flesh in the church (Gal 5:20).

etymology: From the Latin accusatio, from accusare (ad, to, and causa, a cause or suit) — literally to call one to a cause, that is, to summon him to answer at law; it renders the Greek katēgoria, a speaking against in open court, and aitia, the charge or ground of a case.
biblical_def: An accusation is a charge formally laid against a person, calling him to answer. Scripture treats it with the utmost seriousness because a false one can kill and a true one must be answered. Pilate opens the trial of Christ with the proper question: “What accusation bring ye against this man?” (Joh 18:29), and the answer, when it finally came, was nailed above His head: “And set up over his head his accusation written, THIS IS JESUS THE KING OF THE JEWS” (Mat 27:37). The charge on which the Son of God was executed was the truth. Paul guards the church with the Mosaic rule of witnesses: “Against an elder receive not an accusation, but before two or three witnesses” (1Ti 5:19) — a fence against the destruction of a faithful man by rumour. Behind all human accusation stands a spiritual one. Satan is ho katēgōr, the accuser, and Zechariah shows him at his work: Joshua the high priest stands before the angel of the LORD in filthy garments, “and Satan standing at his right hand to resist him” (Zec 3:1). The answer is not a defence of Joshua’s record but a change of clothing: “I have caused thine iniquity to pass from thee, and I will clothe thee with change of raiment” (Zec 3:4). That is justification, and it is why the accuser is at last cast down (Rev 12:10).
webster_summary: A charge brought against a person; in Scripture both the formal indictment at law and the work of Satan, whose accusations are answered by justification in Christ.
webster_full: ACCUSATION, the act of charging with a crime or offence; the charge of an offence or crime, or the declaration containing the charge.
From the Latin accusare, of ad and causa, a cause or suit — to call one to a cause.
In law, a charge brought before a magistrate having jurisdiction, as distinguished from mere censure or reproach.
The Mosaic and apostolic rule required two or three witnesses to establish any accusation (Deu 19:15; 1Ti 5:19).
Applied to the superscription set over our Saviour’s head upon the cross, which declared the charge of His condemnation (Mat 27:37).
scriptures: Pilate then went out unto them, and said, What accusation bring ye against this man?
And set up over his head his accusation written, THIS IS JESUS THE KING OF THE JEWS.
Against an elder receive not an accusation, but before two or three witnesses.

And I heard a loud voice saying in heaven, Now is come salvation, and strength, and the kingdom of our God, and the power of his Christ: for the accuser of our brethren is cast down, which accused them before our God day and night.
corruption_summary: Accusation has been severed from evidence: the charge itself is now treated as the verdict, and the ancient requirement of two or three witnesses is dismissed as an obstacle to justice rather than its foundation.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption abroad is the collapse of the distinction between an accusation and a proof. A charge is published, repeated, and amplified until repetition does the work that evidence used to do, and the accused — who may be entirely innocent — is ruined before any hearing. Scripture has forbidden precisely this from Sinai onward. “At the mouth of two witnesses, or three witnesses, shall he that is worthy of death be put to death; but at the mouth of one witness he shall not be put to death” (Deu 17:6); “one witness shall not rise up against a man for any iniquity” (Deu 19:15). Paul writes the same rule into the church’s discipline of its ministers (1Ti 5:19), and the law of Moses turns the sanction back upon the false accuser, who was to suffer what he sought to inflict (Deu 19:19). None of this is indifference to the wronged; it is the only structure in which the wronged can actually be vindicated. Where accusation alone suffices, the liar is the most powerful person in the room.

The deeper matter is spiritual, and the believer must learn to tell two voices apart. The Spirit convicts of sin specifically, in order to bring a man to repentance and to Christ. The accuser charges generally and endlessly, in order to drive him to despair — and Revelation says he does it “day and night” (Rev 12:10). Zechariah’s vision shows the only sufficient answer: Joshua stands in filthy garments, the accusation is entirely just, and the LORD does not dispute it — He removes the iniquity and clothes the man in change of raiment (Zec 3:4). So the apostle: “Who shall lay any thing to the charge of God’s elect? It is God that justifieth” (Rom 8:33). The accuser is not refuted; he is overruled by the Judge, and cast down by the blood of the Lamb.
roots_summary: Greek katēgoria, a speaking-against in the assembly, gives both the charge and the accuser, katēgōr — Satan’s title in Rev 12:10.
roots_lines: Greek katēgoria (G2724) — from kata, against, and agora, the place of public assembly: a speaking against a man in open court.
Greek aitia (G156) — the cause or ground of a charge; the word on the superscription above the cross (Mat 27:37).
Greek katēgōr (G2725) — the accuser; used of Satan in Rev 12:10, answering the Hebrew sātān, adversary.
Hebrew sātān (H7854) — one who withstands or resists at law, standing at the right hand of the accused (Zec 3:1; Psa 109:6).
Latin accusare, from ad causam — to call a man to his cause; the English keeps the courtroom in the word.
usage: Of the formal charge demanded and recorded at the trial and crucifixion of Christ (Joh 18:29; Mat 27:37).
Of the church’s discipline, where no charge against an elder is received but before two or three witnesses (1Ti 5:19).
Of Satan’s ceaseless work against the brethren, answered by justification and ended by his casting down (Zec 3:1–5; Rev 12:10).

etymology: From the Latin insurrectio, from insurgere (in, upon, and surgere, to rise) — a rising up against; in the New Testament it renders the Greek stasis, the same word rendered “sedition,” and epanistamai, to rise up upon.
biblical_def: An insurrection is an armed or tumultuous rising against established authority. The word carries its full weight at the trial of Christ, where Mark introduces the man who will be released in His place: “And there was one named Barabbas, which lay bound with them that had made insurrection with him, who had committed murder in the insurrection” (Mar 15:7). Here is a man taken in arms, guilty of blood, awaiting execution — and the multitude, offered a choice, ask for him. Pilate delivers Jesus to their will and looses the murderer (Luk 23:25). The exchange is not incidental to the passion narrative; it is the passion narrative in miniature. The guilty man goes free because the innocent Man is condemned in his room, and every sinner saved by Christ can put his own name where Barabbas stood. The word appears elsewhere in plain civil usage: the Jews at Corinth “made insurrection with one accord against Paul, and brought him to the judgment seat” (Act 18:12), and David prays to be hidden “from the insurrection of the workers of iniquity” (Psa 64:2). Scripture never romanticises the risen mob. Yet it insists that God governs even the tumult: the rulers took counsel together against the LORD and against His Anointed, and did only what God’s hand and counsel determined before to be done (Act 4:26–28).
webster_summary: A rising against civil or political authority; the open resistance of a body of men to lawful government, of which Barabbas was guilty and Christ was not.
webster_full: INSURRECTION, a rising against civil or political authority; the open and active opposition of a number of persons to the execution of law.
From the Latin insurgere, of in and surgo, to rise.
It is distinguished from rebellion, which is an insurrection of greater extent and design, aiming to overthrow the government itself.
In the New Testament it renders stasis, a standing off or faction, the crime charged against Barabbas (Mar 15:7).
Also used of a tumultuous rising against a person, as the Jews at Corinth rose against Paul (Act 18:12).
scriptures: Mar 15:7
And there was one named Barabbas, which lay bound with them that had made insurrection with him, who had committed murder in the insurrection.
And he released unto them him that for sedition and murder was cast into prison, whom they had desired; but he delivered Jesus to their will.
And when Gallio was the deputy of Achaia, the Jews made insurrection with one accord against Paul, and brought him to the judgment seat,
Psa 64:2
Hide me from the secret counsel of the wicked; from the insurrection of the workers of iniquity:
corruption_summary: Liberation theology rehabilitates Barabbas as a freedom fighter and recasts Christ as a failed revolutionary — erasing the substitution the exchange was staged to display.
corruption_paragraphs: The characteristic modern misreading of Mar 15:7 comes from liberation theology and its descendants, which read Barabbas as a patriot resisting Roman occupation and press Jesus into the same mould — a political insurgent whose kingdom was earthly and whose cross was a revolutionary’s defeat. The text will not carry it. Mark does not call Barabbas a patriot; he says he “had committed murder in the insurrection” (Mar 15:7). And Christ, standing before Pilate on precisely this charge, answers it directly: “My kingdom is not of this world: if my kingdom were of this world, then would my servants fight” (Joh 18:36). To turn the Lord of glory into a political revolutionary is to lose the atonement altogether, for a martyr for a cause does not bear sin. The whole point of the scene is that the two men are opposites and that they trade places.

Read it as Scripture stages it, and the courtyard preaches. Barabbas is guilty, condemned, and has no defence; Jesus is innocent, and Pilate says so three times (Luk 23:4, 14, 22). The crowd chooses, the governor yields, and the guilty man walks out through a door opened by another man’s condemnation. This is substitution enacted in public before it is expounded in the epistles: “For Christ also hath once suffered for sins, the just for the unjust, that he might bring us to God” (1Pe 3:18). Nor was it an accident of Roman politics. The apostles prayed afterward that Herod and Pilate and the Gentiles and the people were gathered together “For to do whatsoever thy hand and thy counsel determined before to be done” (Act 4:28). The insurrection of the workers of iniquity accomplished the decree of God, and the sinner’s release was purchased at the bar.
roots_summary: Latin insurgere, to rise upon; Greek stasis and epanistamai — the picture is of men rising up against a head set over them.
roots_lines: Latin insurgere — in, upon, and surgere, to rise; whence also insurgent and surge.
Greek stasis (G4714) — a standing off, faction, riot; the same noun rendered “sedition” at Luk 23:19.
Greek sustasiastēs (G4955) — a fellow-insurgent; those bound with Barabbas in Mar 15:7.
Hebrew rigshāh (H7285), in Psa 64:2, a tumultuous throng — the same root as the raging heathen of Psa 2:1.
Aramaic ’eshtaddūr in Ezra’s letters is rendered “insurrection” of the rebuilt city — the standing charge against Jerusalem.
usage: Of the crime of Barabbas, the murderer released while the innocent Christ was condemned (Mar 15:7; Luk 23:25).
Of a tumultuous rising against a servant of God, as at Corinth before Gallio’s judgment seat (Act 18:12).
Of the ragings of the wicked from which the psalmist seeks hiding in God (Psa 64:2).

etymology: From the Old English stocc, “a stump, log, or block of wood”; the instrument was a heavy timber bored to receive the feet, so that the prisoner was fixed and shamed at once. It renders the Hebrew mahpēketh (a thing that twists or distorts) and sad, and the Greek xylon, simply “wood.”
biblical_def: The stocks were a wooden frame that clamped a prisoner’s feet — sometimes the neck and hands as well — holding him bent and immovable in a public place. It was punishment and public shame together, and Scripture shows it fastened upon righteous men. Pashur the priest, chief governor in the house of the LORD, “smote Jeremiah the prophet, and put him in the stocks that were in the high gate of Benjamin, which was by the house of the LORD” (Jer 20:2). The faithful prophet is punished at the temple gate by the temple officer, and when he is brought forth the next morning he does not recant but prophesies (Jer 20:3). Jeremiah 29:26 shows the practice was routine: the officers of the house were to put “every man that is mad, and maketh himself a prophet” in prison and in the stocks. Job, in his affliction, uses the figure of God Himself: “Thou puttest my feet also in the stocks, and lookest narrowly unto all my paths” (Job 13:27). And the New Testament gives the scene that has cheered the persecuted church ever since. The jailer at Philippi “thrust them into the inner prison, and made their feet fast in the stocks” (Act 16:24) — and then, “at midnight Paul and Silas prayed, and sang praises unto God: and the prisoners heard them” (Act 16:25). Feet fast; mouths free.
webster_summary: A wooden frame with holes to confine the feet of an offender, used for punishment and public shame; the instrument that held Jeremiah at the temple gate and Paul and Silas at Philippi.
webster_full: STOCKS, a machine consisting of two pieces of timber, in which the legs of criminals are confined by way of punishment.
From the Old English stocc, a stump, log, or block of wood.
The punishment was public, joining bodily restraint with open shame before the passers-by.
In the Hebrew, mahpēketh, from a root signifying to overturn or distort, the body being held in a wrenched posture (Jer 20:2).
In the Greek, xylon, wood; used of the instrument at Philippi (Act 16:24).
scriptures: Jer 20:2
Then Pashur smote Jeremiah the prophet, and put him in the stocks that were in the high gate of Benjamin, which was by the house of the LORD.

The LORD hath made thee priest in the stead of Jehoiada the priest, that ye should be officers in the house of the LORD, for every man that is mad, and maketh himself a prophet, that thou shouldest put him in prison, and in the stocks.
Who, having received such a charge, thrust them into the inner prison, and made their feet fast in the stocks.
Thou puttest my feet also in the stocks, and lookest narrowly unto all my paths; thou settest a print upon the heels of my feet.
corruption_summary: A plain instrument of ancient punishment, requiring no modern rescue — but the lesson of the men who sang in it is regularly mislaid.
corruption_paragraphs: The stocks belong to the furniture of the ancient world and pass into Scripture without dispute: a bored timber, two feet, a public place. What deserves notice is not a redefinition but a pattern. In every instance where Scripture names the stocks, the man in them is in the right and the man turning the key is in authority. Pashur was chief governor in the house of the LORD; Jeremiah was the prophet of the LORD; and the stocks stood at the high gate of Benjamin, by the house of the LORD (Jer 20:2). Religious office does not sanctify the officer, and the fact that a punishment is administered by the temple establishment does not make it just. Jeremiah came out of the timber the next morning with a harder word than he had gone in with (Jer 20:3), and the church has needed that example in every century since.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the one Paul and Silas demonstrated at midnight. Their backs were laid open with rods, their feet were fast in the wood, the inner prison was dark, and they “prayed, and sang praises unto God: and the prisoners heard them” (Act 16:25). The singing was not a coping technique; it was worship offered by men who believed that the God who had sent them to Philippi was in the prison with them. The earthquake followed, and the jailer was converted before daylight — not by the deliverance, but by the men. Joy in affliction is a testimony no argument can answer. Recover the plain confidence beneath it: no timber, no magistrate, and no gate of hell can bind the word of God (2Ti 2:9), and the saints may sing in the dark because the outcome was never in the jailer’s hands.
roots_summary: Hebrew mahpēketh, from a root meaning to overturn or wrench; Greek xylon, simply wood — the same word used of the tree on which Christ hung.
roots_lines: Hebrew mahpēketh (H4115) — from hāphak, to overturn or distort; the instrument that wrenched the body (Jer 20:2; Jer 29:26).
Hebrew sad (H5465) — a fetter or block for the feet, used in Job 13:27 and Job 33:11.
Greek xylon (G3586) — wood, timber; the stocks at Philippi (Act 16:24).
The same xylon is the word for the tree on which Christ was hanged (Act 5:30; 1Pe 2:24) — His saints are fastened to wood after Him.
The Old English stocc, a stump or log, gives the plural form the Authorized Version keeps, the frame being made of two timbers.
usage: Of the punishment inflicted upon Jeremiah by Pashur at the high gate of Benjamin (Jer 20:2–3).
Of the routine confinement of any man reckoned mad who made himself a prophet (Jer 29:26).
Of Paul and Silas in the inner prison at Philippi, whose feet were fast while they sang at midnight (Act 16:24–25).
